records.sourceFile: Exploring the role of sprint biomechanics in hamstring strain injuries - A current opinion on existing concepts and evidence.pdf

paper.citation: Bramah C, Mendiguchia J, Dos'Santos T, Morin JB. Exploring the Role of Sprint Biomechanics in Hamstring Strain Injuries: A Current Opinion on Existing Concepts and Evidence. Sports Med. 2023.
paper.abstract: The authors argue that hamstring prevention and rehabilitation have focused on increasing hamstring tolerance to strain while paying little attention to the mechanical strain itself, which sprint mechanics may influence. They review the proposed mechanistic links between sprint running mechanics and hamstring strain, along with the supporting evidence, and identify areas for further research.
paper.tldr: Sprint mechanics such as anterior pelvic tilt, trunk control and over-striding are plausible, partly modifiable contributors to hamstring strain, but the injury evidence for most of them is limited. Staff should treat these as targets for further study, not as proven risk factors.
paper.methods: Current opinion article that reviews functional anatomy, biomechanical modelling, and retrospective and prospective studies on sprint kinematics and hamstring strain injury. No systematic search method is described.
paper.findings: The authors conclude that functional anatomy and modelling studies support a role for sprint mechanics in hamstring tissue strain, but no single biomechanical parameter has been identified as a driver of strain. Anterior pelvic tilt has mixed prospective evidence but a mechanistic link through elastography, and lumbo-pelvic control has supporting prospective and experimental evidence; the links for back-side mechanics, triple extension and lumbar extension are described as theoretical, maximal hip flexion findings conflict across three retrospective studies, and over-striding and forward trunk lean have plausible mechanisms but little injury data. The authors also state that no established in-field method or threshold for normal mechanics exists.
paper.limitations: The review does not describe how its evidence was selected, and the prospective anterior pelvic tilt studies had only four injured players between them, so they are likely underpowered. The authors note that no biomechanical study of lumbar kinematics in hamstring injury exists, and that the evidence for back-side mechanics, triple extension, maximal hip flexion, over-striding and forward lean is conflicting, limited, or theoretical.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff could assess sprint mechanics such as anterior pelvic tilt, trunk control and hip flexion during maximal-speed running as possible modifiable contributors to hamstring strain, alongside eccentric strength work. The authors note that interventions can reduce anterior pelvic tilt during sprinting, but no validated in-field screening method or threshold for normal technique exists, so any target would be provisional.
paper.athleteDev: Sprint technique such as anterior pelvic tilt, trunk control and over-striding could be observed as possible modifiable contributors to hamstring strain in sprint-based training. No validated in-field assessment or threshold for normal technique exists, so any technique target would be provisional.
paper.rtp: The authors suggest that targeting sprint mechanics may help hamstring rehabilitation, but they present this as an area for further study. The review reports no rehabilitation outcomes and sets no return-to-sport criteria, so it should not be used to judge return-to-sport timing or clearance.

paper.citation: Ziedas A, Nasir M, Dubé M, Elagamy N, Gumma J, Shaheen P, et al. Full Return to Sport After Suture-Button Fixation for Syndesmotic Injuries in All Athletes; However, Faster Recovery Was Seen in National Collegiate Athletic Association Football Players Compared with National Football League Players. Arthroscopy, Sports Medicine, and Rehabilitation. 2025.
paper.abstract: This retrospective cohort study included 21 ankles in 7 NCAA and 14 NFL football players treated with suture-button fixation for unstable syndesmotic injuries between 2017 and 2023, using public data. Only players who returned to NCAA or NFL play were included; NCAA players returned sooner, and postinjury game totals per season were similar in both groups.
paper.tldr: In this small public-record series of football players who all returned after suture-button fixation for a syndesmotic ankle injury, NCAA players returned in about 39 days and NFL players in about 190 days. Because non-returners were excluded, the study gives return times for returners, not a return-to-play rate, and it cannot explain the NCAA versus NFL difference.
paper.methods: Retrospective cohort study (Level III). NCAA and NFL players with in-season syndesmotic injuries treated with suture-button fixation were identified from public sources, and each injury was cross-referenced with at least two sources. Players were excluded if the injury or surgery could not be verified, if they had not played a game before the injury, or if they did not return to NCAA or NFL play. Time to first game, games played per season before and after injury, age, BMI and position were compared using t-tests and chi-square or Fisher's exact tests, with P < 0.05 as significant.
paper.findings: All 21 included ankles returned to sport, as required for inclusion. Mean time from surgery to first game was 139.4 ± 123.6 days (range 12 to 427). Time to return was shorter in NCAA players (39.0 ± 20.4 days) than NFL players (189.6 ± 123.2 days; P = 0.005). Postinjury games per season were 8.6 ± 4.6 (NCAA, including later NFL games) and 11.2 ± 5.9 (NFL), P = 0.32. NCAA players were younger (20.0 ± 1.2 versus 27.3 ± 3.6 years, P < 0.001) and had fewer preinjury games per season (8.6 ± 1.7 versus 13.5 ± 2.0, P < 0.001).
paper.limitations: Players who did not return to play were excluded, so the 100% return rate is built into the design and the Discussion's comparisons with return rates after ACL reconstruction are not valid. The sample is small (7 NCAA and 14 NFL players), and injury, surgery and return data came from public reports rather than medical records, so selection and inaccuracy bias are possible. The study did not measure individual performance statistics, PROMs or ankle function scores, did not control for rehabilitation, and the Discussion's claim that the procedure does not compromise athletic performance goes beyond what games played can show.
paper.practicalImplications: This study cannot be used to say how likely a football player is to return after suture-button fixation, because only players who returned were studied. Among those who did return, time to first game ranged from 12 to 427 days and differed by about five months between NCAA and NFL players, so return timelines should be planned individually; the study cannot say which factors caused the difference.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application is limited. The study counts games played and does not measure sport-specific performance, so it cannot show that the technique preserves training or competitive output.
paper.rtp: For players who do return after suture-button fixation, this series shows a wide range of times to first game (12 to 427 days) and similar games per season after return. It cannot give a return-to-play rate or set return criteria, because non-returners were excluded and rehabilitation, functional testing and PROMs were not recorded.

records.sourceFile: Factors Associated with Persisting Post-Concussion Symptoms Among Collegiate Athletes and Military Cadets - Findings from the NCAA-DoD CARE Consortium.pdf

paper.citation: Rooks LT, Bertò G, Pasquina PF, Broglio SP, McAllister TW, McCrea MA, et al. Factors Associated with Persisting Post-Concussion Symptoms Among Collegiate Athletes and Military Cadets: Findings from the NCAA-DoD CARE Consortium. Sports Medicine. 2025.
paper.abstract: This analysis of 5,073 concussions from the NCAA-DoD CARE Consortium examined which pre-injury and post-injury factors were linked to slow recovery, defined as return to play after more than 29 days. A high early symptom score, three or more prior concussions, female sex and delayed reporting were associated with slower recovery in the adjusted model, while NCAA sport participation (compared with cadets) and injury at practice or competition (compared with outside sport) were associated with lower odds.
paper.tldr: In this large collegiate and cadet concussion dataset, a high early symptom score, three or more prior concussions, female sex and delayed reporting were linked to return to play after more than 29 days. A prognostic model built from these factors missed 91% of athletes with slow recovery.
paper.methods: Analysis of prospectively collected CARE Consortium data from 30 sites (2014 to 2019); nonsport cadets were excluded. Baseline histories and SCAT3 and BSI-18 scores were used with post-injury symptom scores taken within 48 hours. Outcomes were days to return to play (Cox models) and return to play after more than 29 days (PPCS, logistic models). Adjusted odds ratios came from stepwise logistic regression (stepAIC), checked with LASSO, with cadets and outside-of-sport injury as reference categories. Missing data were excluded from each analysis.
paper.findings: Median and mean return to play were 15.2 and 22.2 days, and 891 athletes took more than 29 days. Adjusted odds ratios were: SCAT symptom total above 45 (OR 1.91, 95% CI 1.58 to 2.30), three or more prior concussions (OR 1.80, 1.29 to 2.52), female sex (OR 1.80, 1.53 to 2.13) and delayed reporting (OR 1.42, 1.20 to 1.67). Contact (OR 0.34), limited-contact (0.34) and noncontact sport (0.35) were lower relative to cadets, and injury at practice (0.64) or in competition (0.44) relative to injury outside sport; with cadets removed, noncontact (OR 1.79) and limited-contact (1.32) sport had higher odds than the reference and contact sport lower (0.62). Learning disability with a neurostimulant (unadjusted OR 0.44) and learning disability overall (0.59) were not retained in the adjusted model, and the nine-variable prognostic model had an AUC of 0.72, sensitivity 9% and specificity 98%.
paper.limitations: Mental health, migraine, learning disability, prior concussion and LOC were self-reported, and the BSI-18 and SCAT symptom scores are subjective. Return to play depends on staff decisions and season timing, so it is a weak proxy for symptom resolution, and exposure was not measured. The high-symptom threshold is given as SCAT above 45 in the text but as SCAT 68 or higher in Figures 2 and 3, and the neurostimulant recommendation in the abstract and conclusions rests on unadjusted odds ratios that were removed from the adjusted model.
paper.practicalImplications: A high SCAT symptom score within 48 hours, three or more prior concussions, female sex and delayed reporting can help flag athletes who may need closer follow-up. The prognostic model should not be used to predict individual outcome, since it detected only 9% of athletes with return to play after 29 days, and the study does not support medication decisions.
paper.athleteDev: The study does not address training or performance outcomes. Its results relate to recovery timing after concussion and should not be used to judge performance load.
paper.rtp: The findings can inform cautious return-to-play planning by showing which early factors were linked to longer times, but the study does not test a return protocol. The authors' outcome is clinician-cleared return to play after 29 days, so it cannot set clearance criteria for an individual athlete.

records.sourceFile: Fantasy Points associated with professional athlete performance after lumbar discectomy or microdiscectomy.pdf

paper.citation: Kajy M, Higginbotham DO, Ball G, Vaidya R. "Fantasy Points" associated with Professional Athlete Performance after Lumbar Discectomy or Microdiscectomy. Spartan Medical Research Journal. 2022;7(1).
paper.abstract: This retrospective series of 38 professional players from the NFL, NBA, NHL and MLB who had a lumbar discectomy or microdiscectomy used fantasy points or WAR to compare performance before and after surgery. Return to play was 82% overall, with NFL players the least likely to return, and the authors report a long-term decline in performance after surgery.
paper.tldr: Most professional players in this public-record series returned to play after a lumbar discectomy, but their fantasy points and WAR tended to fall in the years that followed. The series has no control group, so the decline cannot be attributed to surgery.
paper.methods: Retrospective series of professional players who missed at least one game after a lumbar discectomy or microdiscectomy between 1993 and 2015. Data came from public sites including ESPN, Rotoworld and FanGraphs. Fantasy points (NFL, NBA, NHL) and WAR (MLB) were tabulated per season, with pre- and post-surgery averages compared. Return to play, career length after surgery, time to pre-surgery performance level and recovery time were summarised descriptively, with no statistical testing or control group.
paper.findings: Of 38 players, 31 (82%) returned to play: NFL 9 of 14 (64%), NBA 6 of 7 (86%), NHL 8 of 9 (89%), MLB 7 of 8 (88%). Average recovery time was 6 months (NFL), 2.8 months (NBA), 4.7 months (NHL) and 12 months (MLB). Ten of 14 NFL players (71%) had fewer games played and lower fantasy scores after surgery, as did 4 of 7 NBA players, 4 of 9 NHL players (6 of 9 with lower fantasy value) and 7 of 8 MLB players. Twelve players (31%) improved in the first two years after surgery before declining.
paper.limitations: The sample is small and male-only, has no age-matched controls, and relies on public sources that may be inaccurate; no statistical tests were run, and careers continuing after 2015 were cut short. Table 3 gives one example NFL player's averages (games 14.63 to 13.5, fantasy 73.94 to 43.63), but the Discussion presents these as averages for all players who returned, which the data do not support. The abstract calls the NFL career length (34.8 months) the lowest, but Table 4 shows NHL players lowest at 29 months.
paper.practicalImplications: The study is useful as a description of return-to-play and performance trends in elite players after lumbar discectomy, and it suggests that performance may not return to pre-surgery levels in some players. Staff should not treat the performance decline as a surgical effect, since no controls were used.
paper.athleteDev: The performance metrics in this study are measures of game production, not training outcomes. Staff could use the pattern of post-surgery change to set expectations for playing time, but the study does not address how training should change after surgery.
paper.rtp: The return-to-play rates (82% overall, 64% in NFL players) and recovery times (2.8 to 12 months) in this series can inform expectations for elite players after lumbar discectomy. The study cannot set criteria for return, because the surgical and clinical details that drive clearance were limited and not controlled.

records.sourceFile: Fascia and Muscle Stiffness in Soccer Athletes with and Without Previous Hamstring Injury.pdf

paper.citation: Kellis E, Kekelekis A, Drakonaki EE. Fascia and Muscle Stiffness in Soccer Athletes with and Without Previous Hamstring Injury. J. Funct. Morphol. Kinesiol. 2025;10:48.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study compared fascia and muscle stiffness, measured with shear-wave elastography, in 10 soccer players with a previous biceps femoris strain and 13 uninjured players. Active stiffness during submaximal contraction was higher in the injured group, while passive stiffness was similar, and the injured group had lower strength and biceps femoris cross-sectional area.
paper.tldr: Soccer players about four months after a grade II biceps femoris strain had stiffer fascia and muscle than uninjured players, but only during contraction. They were also weaker and had less biceps femoris muscle area.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional study of semi-professional soccer players recruited from eight Greek clubs. Ten players with an MRI or ultrasound-confirmed grade II biceps femoris long head strain within the past year who had returned to play (4 recurrent injuries; mean 34.8 days lost) and 13 age-matched uninjured players were tested. Shear-wave elastography of the semitendinosus and biceps femoris fascia and muscle was measured passively and at 60% MVC at 0, 45 and 90 degrees of knee flexion, with surface EMG and isometric MVC from a hand-held dynamometer. Cross-sectional area was measured in 8 injured and 12 uninjured players, and four-way ANOVA and t-tests were used.
paper.findings: Group effect on SWE modulus averaged across conditions was significant (F1,21 = 4.91, P = 0.038), with the group by condition interaction significant (P = 0.018). Post hoc tests found higher stiffness in the injured group during active contraction only. Injured players had lower MVC at all three angles (for example 93.4 vs 122.8 Nm at 0 degrees) and lower biceps femoris cross-sectional area (13.2 vs 14.6 cm2, P = 0.012). Normalised EMG did not differ between groups (P > 0.05). Reliability of the SWE measures was high (ICC 0.86 to 0.94).
paper.limitations: The sample is small and homogeneous (one sport, one injury grade, one muscle), the groups were matched only on age, and rehabilitation and injury mechanism were not controlled. The cross-sectional design cannot show whether stiffness was caused by the injury or existed before it. The Results text says MVC was greater in the injured group, but Table 3 and the abstract show it was lower, and the text says the semitendinosus was stiffer than the biceps femoris while Table 1 reports ST < BF.
paper.practicalImplications: Players who return to play after a biceps femoris strain may show higher stiffness during active contraction, along with lower strength and muscle area. Staff may want to check strength and muscle size in addition to standard return-to-play measures. The study does not show that treating fascia stiffness reduces re-injury.
paper.athleteDev: The study does not test any training intervention. Injured players had lower knee flexor strength and biceps femoris area, which the authors attribute to atrophy rather than lower activation, but the study cannot show that strength training restores fascia stiffness or performance.
paper.rtp: Injured players in this study, at a mean of about four months after a biceps femoris strain and after returning to play, had higher active fascia and muscle stiffness, lower strength and lower biceps femoris area. The study does not provide return-to-play criteria, and the authors suggest that management may be needed for about six months after injury without evidence that it prevents recurrence.

records.sourceFile: Fascial tissue research in sports medicine- from molecules to tissue adaptation, injury and diagnostics.pdf

paper.citation: Zügel M, Maganaris CN, Wilke J, Jurkat-Rott K, Klingler W, Wearing SC, et al. Fascial tissue research in sports medicine: from molecules to tissue adaptation, injury and diagnostics. Br J Sports Med. 2018.
paper.abstract: A consensus statement from the Second International CONNECT Conference and a follow-up expert meeting on fascial tissue in sports medicine. It reviews the fascial system from molecular and cellular responses to mechanical properties, the responses of fascia to exercise, disuse, injury, ageing and inflammation, the methods used to study fascia, and interventions that target fascial tissue in sport and exercise.
paper.tldr: Fascial tissue responds to loading, injury and ageing, but the diagnostic methods for it have limited reliability and validity, and treatment evidence is still incomplete. Use the statement to frame fascia as a tissue to consider in injury and rehabilitation, and treat claims for specific fascia treatments with caution.
paper.methods: Consensus statement developed from the Second International CONNECT Conference (Ulm, Germany, March 2017) and a follow-up meeting of conference speakers and experts. The Methods section does not describe a systematic search or formal consensus procedure.
paper.findings: The authors report that tendon stiffness increases with chronic overloading and decreases with chronic unloading, with adaptations occurring within weeks, and that changes in tendon size and Young's modulus both contribute. They report that injury or overload triggers an inflammatory response that, if prolonged, can produce fibrosis and fatty change, and that resistance exercise is needed to reverse fatty change in chronic muscle conditions. They also report that manual palpation and bioimpedance have limited reliability, and that ultrasound-based stiffness estimates often disagree with in vitro material tests.
paper.limitations: The statement does not describe how the consensus was reached, and only some claims carry an evidence grade (for example, moderate evidence for shockwave therapy and eccentric loading in tendon healing). Much of the mechanistic evidence comes from animal, cadaver or in vitro work, and the authors state that the contribution of myofascial force transmission under in vivo conditions remains to be elucidated.
paper.practicalImplications: Treat fascial stiffness and tissue-change measures as limited in accuracy: the authors advise interpreting clinical soft-tissue data with caution and combining methods while no gold standard exists. They report that resistance exercise is needed to reverse fatty change in chronic muscle conditions, and that anti-inflammatory drugs used for overuse pathologies may impair regeneration and diminish tissue adaptation. Foam rolling may help short-term flexibility and soreness, but manual therapies such as massage, osteopathy and Rolfing are not yet validated.
paper.athleteDev: The statement supports the view that tendons adapt to chronic loading and unloading within weeks, so progressive loading of connective tissue is the relevant mechanism. It gives no dose or programme for athletes, and it reports only short-term flexibility and soreness benefits for foam rolling.
paper.rtp: The statement can support the view that fascial tissue changes after injury, such as fibrosis and fatty infiltration, may persist and affect function. It does not establish a return-to-sport threshold or validated tests for judging fascial recovery.

records.sourceFile: Fatigue induced changes in hamstrings' active muscle stiffness - Effect of contraction type and implications for strain injuries.pdf

paper.citation: Evangelidis PE, Shan X, Otsuka S, Yang C, Yamagishi T, Kawakami Y. Fatigue-induced changes in hamstrings' active muscle stiffness: effect of contraction type and implications for strain injuries. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2022.
paper.abstract: The authors examined the effect of a submaximal fatiguing task on hamstring active muscle stiffness, measured by shear wave velocity, and whether contraction type (isometric, concentric or eccentric) changes this effect. Nine healthy males completed 99 submaximal knee flexions in each mode. Shear wave velocity was measured during contraction in the biceps femoris long head, semitendinosus and semimembranosus, and T2 relaxation was measured by MRI before and after the task. Stiffness responses differed by muscle and contraction type, and the authors report preliminary evidence that the biceps femoris long head is more fatigued during eccentric contractions.
paper.tldr: Fatigue changed the stiffness of individual hamstring muscles differently depending on contraction type. In this small study of healthy men, biceps femoris long head stiffness fell after eccentric fatigue, a pattern that may be relevant to why that muscle is injured, but the study did not measure injury.
paper.methods: Within-subject laboratory study. Nine healthy males (age 21.8 +/- 4.2 years) completed one session in each of isometric, concentric and eccentric modes, with 99 contractions at 50% maximal voluntary torque. Shear wave velocity was recorded during contraction for three hamstring muscles, and maximal voluntary torque and T2 MRI were measured before and after the task, with a 48-hour follow-up.
paper.findings: Maximal voluntary torque fell after all three tasks: isometric -18.4%, concentric -33.6% and eccentric -30.9% (pre to post). Average relative torque during the task was lower in concentric (41.9% MVT) than isometric (49.1%) and eccentric (46.5%), while absolute torque was similar. Biceps femoris long head shear wave velocity fell after eccentric fatigue (-0.8 m/s, -7.7%, p < 0.01) and tended to rise after isometric fatigue (+0.4 m/s, +4.5%, p = 0.064). Semitendinosus (-1.1 m/s, -9.0%) and semimembranosus (-0.8 m/s, -8.1%) velocity fell after concentric fatigue. T2 rose after the task and returned to baseline by 48 hours.
paper.limitations: The sample of nine was small and the authors state that they used a more qualitative interpretation of the data. Individual stiffness responses were highly variable, and the ANOVA found no significant pairwise differences between contraction types and no contraction type by muscle interaction, so the contrasts rest on within-condition changes. Relative torque during the task differed between conditions, the task intensity was moderate, and participants were healthy young men without hamstring injury history, with no injury outcomes measured.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff who assess fatigue of the hamstrings may need to test contraction types that match the sport's demands, because the study found different responses by contraction type. Eccentric fatigue was associated with reduced biceps femoris long head stiffness in this sample, which the authors link to strain injury risk. The study does not show that any load management strategy reduces injury.
paper.athleteDev: The study suggests that the same fatiguing work can change hamstring muscles differently depending on contraction type, so fatigue monitoring may need to consider eccentric demands. It does not test a training or recovery intervention, and its participants were healthy young men who were not described as athletes.
paper.rtp: The study does not address return to sport, because it included no injured participants and no return-to-play outcomes. It suggests a possible mechanism that would need testing in injured athletes before it could inform return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Fibrosis and Sports Injuries - Concept and Implications - The GESMUTE-SETRADE Consensus Statement.pdf

paper.citation: Beas-Jiménez JD, León Garrigosa A, Doñoro Cuevas P, Álvarez Recio MI, Cofré Bolados C, Alonso JM. Fibrosis and Sports Injuries: Concept and Implications. The GESMUTE-SETRADE Consensus Statement. Orthop J Sports Med. 2024;12(9):23259671241266604.
paper.abstract: Consensus statement by the GESMUTE and SETRADE groups, based on a bibliographic review, that proposes a definition of musculoskeletal fibrosis in sport. The authors define fibrosis as an abnormal accumulation of extracellular matrix, usually a complication of injury, affecting muscles, tendons, ligaments, joint capsules and nerves, which impairs recovery, causes symptoms and can lead to relapse. The statement also lists sport-related entities in which fibrosis may be present and identifies gaps in epidemiology, diagnosis and treatment.
paper.tldr: Fibrosis after sports injury has no agreed definition, and this statement proposes one: an abnormal build-up of extracellular matrix after injury that can impair recovery and cause relapse. Use it as a working definition for clinical discussion, not as a validated diagnostic standard.
paper.methods: Expert consensus by a Spanish working group. The Methods section describes a bibliographic review of existing scientific evidence and consensus on fibrosis in sport; no search strategy or formal consensus procedure is reported.
paper.findings: The authors report that only one tendon study and four muscle studies have examined fibrosis in post-injury scar tissue, with incidence ranging from 29.5% to 78% on MR or ultrasound. They list entities where fibrosis may be accepted in sport, including granulomas, encapsulated hematomas, tendon and ligament scars, and retractile capsulitis. They state that imaging by ultrasound or MR should confirm fibrosis, and that prior drug treatments (indomethacin, losartan, curcumin, chitosan) have shown very poor outcomes.
paper.limitations: This is expert opinion built on a bibliographic review, with no primary data and no validation of the definition. The authors state that the epidemiology, diagnosis and treatment of sport-related fibrosis remain largely unstudied, and that the effects of exercise type and load programming on fibrosis are unclear.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can use the proposed definition to describe post-injury fibrosis and consider ultrasound or MR to confirm it. The authors' main prevention message is that preventing injury and treating it early and adequately are the most effective measures. No validated treatment for fibrosis is established.
paper.athleteDev: The statement gives no training prescription. For performance staff, its relevance is that fibrosis can persist in muscle, tendon and ligament after injury and can compromise function and regeneration, which the authors link to recurrent injury. It does not show that any training method prevents fibrosis.
paper.rtp: Supports imaging to confirm fibrosis after an injury when a clinician is assessing tissue recovery. It cannot set a return-to-sport threshold, and it does not show that fibrosis changes return-to-play outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Fifth metatarsal strain distribution during cutting motions in soccer.pdf

paper.citation: Miyazaki Y, Sugizaki R, Kawasaki M, Nakagawa T, Saho Y, Tateishi T. Fifth metatarsal strain distribution during cutting motions in soccer. Sports Biomechanics. 2023.
paper.abstract: The authors determined fifth metatarsal strain generation during cutting motions in soccer using a finite element foot model. Five collegiate players performed side-step and cross-step cutting while three-dimensional foot kinematics, ground reaction force and plantar pressure were measured, and these were used as boundary conditions for simulations. During side-step cutting, maximum principal strain on the fifth metatarsal correlated with forefoot adduction during stepping out. During cross-step cutting, it correlated with plantar pressure at the distal end of the fifth metatarsal.
paper.tldr: In five collegiate soccer players, a finite element foot model suggests that fifth metatarsal strain in side-step cutting tracks forefoot adduction, while in cross-step cutting it tracks plantar pressure under the distal fifth metatarsal. These are model-based mechanisms that have not been tested for injury prevention in athletes.
paper.methods: Five male collegiate players performed side-step and cross-step cutting on long-pile artificial turf in a laboratory, with motion capture, force plates and insole pressure sensors. Three trials per player were analysed after two outliers were excluded. A CT-based foot model, with fifth metatarsal stiffness assigned from Hounsfield units across ten levels, was driven by each player's measured foot motion and plantar load. Cross-correlation and Kruskal-Wallis tests with Conover post hoc tests compared strain waveforms with plantar pressure in 13 areas and with forefoot adduction angle.
paper.findings: In side-step cutting, forefoot adduction angle had the highest cross-correlation with fifth metatarsal strain (mean 0.965, SD 0.034). Plantar pressure correlations were lower than adduction, highest in Areas 5 and 6 under the first metatarsal and lowest in Areas 10 and 13 under the fifth metatarsal. In cross-step cutting, plantar pressure in Area 10 under the distal fifth metatarsal had the highest correlation (mean 0.971, SD 0.024), while the adduction angle correlation was low. Kruskal-Wallis tests showed differences among the 14 parameters for both steps (p = 1.96 × 10-5 for cross-step; p = 0.013 for side-step).
paper.limitations: The sample was five players, and the finite element model was built from the CT image of one foot rather than each player's own foot. The study used training shoes without studs on one artificial turf, and stud placement, upper design and surface type were not varied. The authors note that wire-element ligaments concentrate stress at attachment points, that tangential loads were distributed in proportion to plantar pressure, and that bone stiffness was derived from CT values without a calibration phantom; validation used cadaver data from the first and second metatarsals and barefoot adduction in one participant.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors propose that for side-step cutting, shoe uppers that limit forefoot bending and insoles or outsoles that reduce pressure under the first metatarsal may reduce strain. For cross-step cutting, they propose reducing pressure under the distal fifth metatarsal. These proposals come from model results and have not been tested in athletes.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can see that footwear, insole and surface choices change forefoot plantar load, which the authors link to fifth metatarsal strain in simulation. The paper gives no training or conditioning prescription and does not show that any footwear or insole change lowers fracture rates.
paper.rtp: Relevant to fifth metatarsal fracture mechanisms and prevention. It cannot guide return-to-play decisions after a fracture and does not test whether any footwear or insole change reduces re-injury.

records.sourceFile: Foot strike angle as key predictor of multi-plane knee joint moments in sidestep cutting - Implications for ACL injury prevention.pdf

paper.citation: Bill K, Krosshaug T, Kersting UG. Foot strike angle as key predictor of multi-plane knee joint moments in sidestep cutting: implications for ACL injury prevention. Sports Biomechanics. 2025.
paper.abstract: Investigates whether knee joint moments are related to foot strike angle at initial ground contact in pre-planned and unplanned handball sidestep cuts performed by 51 female handball players. Canonical correlation analysis on the three-dimensional knee moment vector field showed a relationship with foot strike angle in both conditions. The authors conclude that single-plane analyses only partly explain this relationship, and that changing foot strike may help reduce multi-plane knee loading linked to ACL injury.
paper.tldr: In female handball players, a more forefoot foot strike angle was associated with knee moment patterns linked to ACL loading during sidestep cuts, most clearly when the three knee moment planes are analysed together. Because these are correlations from unmanipulated cutting, the result supports testing forefoot-strike technique work in prospective studies rather than confirming an injury benefit.
paper.methods: Laboratory study in which 51 high-level female handball players performed at least five valid pre-planned and five unplanned sidestep cuts on a force plate, with a 24-camera motion capture system and full-body marker set. Knee moments were resolved into a three-component vector field over stance, and canonical correlation analysis (statistical parametric mapping) tested its relationship with foot strike angle, followed by post hoc analyses of moment couples and individual components.
paper.findings: Foot strike angle was related to the knee moment vector field in pre-planned cuts during early (0 to 13.2% of stance, p=0.006) and late stance (p=0.029), and in unplanned cuts during early stance (0 to 22.9%, p<0.001) and late stance (p=0.048). The non-sagittal (Mxz) and non-frontal (Myz) moment couples explained most of the early-stance relationship in both conditions. Among individual components, the transverse plane moment (Mz) showed the strongest correlation with foot strike angle (early stance p=0.007 in both conditions), and the authors report that increasing foot strike angle toward a forefoot strike was related to lower internal rotation moments in the peak loading phase, while the abduction moment relationship was not significant.
paper.limitations: No injury data were collected, and the authors state that prospective studies are needed to establish a causal link with injury risk. The study included only female handball players, so generalization to males or other sports is unknown. Foot strike angle was not controlled or manipulated, cutting angles and approach speeds varied, and the authors note that the reasons for larger discrepancies between the vector and single-plane analyses in the unplanned condition are unclear. The study was part of a larger project and the sample size was based on resource constraints rather than a power analysis. The authors consider the late-stance correlations most likely irrelevant to non-contact ACL injury, and the reported late-stance interval for the pre-planned Mz result is printed as '73.8-6.6%', an apparent typo.
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches and clinicians can consider foot strike angle as one technique factor in cutting when assessing knee loading, while recognizing that these are correlations rather than effects of a training intervention. Because single-plane knee moments may understate the multi-plane loading linked to ACL injury, practitioners may need to interpret moment results with a three-dimensional view. Forefoot-strike technique work should be evaluated in intervention studies before it is relied on to reduce injury risk.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: foot strike angle in sidestep cutting was linked to knee loading in female handball players. The authors suggest that the possible performance benefits of a forefoot strike, which this study did not measure, may help athletes accept the technique change; the study does not show that changing foot strike improves cutting performance or reduces injury.
paper.rtp: Limited application: the study examined healthy, injury-free players and did not assess athletes returning from ACL or other injury. It cannot support return-to-sport decisions, although it may inform the technique side of later ACL prevention work.

records.sourceFile: Frontal plane pelvic kinematics during high velocity running - Association with hamstring injury history.pdf

paper.citation: Nurse CA, Lewis CL, Shefelbine SJ. Frontal plane pelvic kinematics during high velocity running: Association with hamstring injury history. Phys Ther Sport. 2023;64:133-139.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study compared frontal-plane pelvic motion during sprinting in 22 NCAA Division 1 sprinters and 17 controls who were not Division 1 athletes, using three inertial measurement units on the pelvis. Sprinters with a hamstring injury in the previous two seasons showed greater mediolateral pelvic motion and side-to-side pelvic asymmetry during stance than healthy sprinters. The authors suggest these differences may matter for rehabilitation, and they note the design cannot show whether they caused or resulted from injury.
paper.tldr: In a small study, sprinters with a recent hamstring injury showed more side-to-side pelvic asymmetry and mediolateral motion during stance than healthy sprinters. The authors suggest postural control and stability work may be worth targeting in rehabilitation, but the design cannot show cause.
paper.methods: Sprinters (12 with a hamstring injury in the previous two seasons, 10 healthy) and non-track controls (17, of whom 3 had a previous hamstring injury) each completed three 50 m sprints with three inertial measurement units on the sacrum and both iliac crests, sampled at 128 Hz. Mediolateral motion was the root-mean-square ratio of sacral mediolateral acceleration, and asymmetry was the difference in vertical acceleration between iliac crest sensors during single-leg stance. Groups were compared with a three-way repeated-measures ANOVA (sex, competitive status, injury history) and Cohen's d.
paper.findings: The authors report higher mediolateral motion during stance in previously injured than in healthy sprinters (p = 0.02, d = 0.93) and more mediolateral motion in controls than in sprinters (p = 0.04, d = 0.41), with no significant sex difference. Pelvic asymmetry was higher in previously injured than in healthy sprinters (p < 0.001, d = 1.39), controls showed larger asymmetry than sprinters (p < 0.001, d = 0.25), and most sprinter outliers were previously injured. The p values come from the injury-history and competitive-status factors of a three-way ANOVA (Table 1).
paper.limitations: The study is cross-sectional with small groups, and the authors state that it cannot show whether the differences contributed to or resulted from injury. Injury history came from a survey, controls were non-competitive participants with only 3 previously injured, so the injury effect rests mainly on the sprinters. The 128 Hz sampling rate may be low for ground contact in sprinting, though the authors argue the effect is small, and no rehabilitation history was available.
paper.practicalImplications: IMU-based pelvic measures were collected in a track setting and may be used for on-the-spot screening, as the authors propose. Treat a high mediolateral motion or asymmetry reading as a prompt for a closer look at lumbo-pelvic strength and coordination, not as a diagnosis or clearance decision. Do not apply the group values to an individual athlete until the findings are confirmed in larger, longitudinal samples.
paper.athleteDev: Side-to-side pelvic symmetry during sprint running may be one way to monitor stance mechanics in sprinters with a hamstring history. The study does not test whether changing these measures improves sprint performance, so pair them with sprint performance data.
paper.rtp: The authors suggest that side-to-side lumbo-pelvic strength and coordination assessment could help confirm readiness to return to sport. The study did not test return-to-sport decisions or outcomes, so these pelvic measures should not be used as return-to-sport clearance criteria.

records.sourceFile: Functional and anatomical characteristics of the heel fat pad based on different sports events.pdf

paper.citation: Maemichi T, Matsumoto M, Okunuki T, Tsutsui T, Kumai T. Functional and anatomical characteristics of the heel fat pad based on different sports events. J Biomech. 2026;196:113148.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study compared heel fat pad thickness and stiffness in 34 male university athletes from judo (barefoot), American football (shoe-based) and swimming (water-based), and in 12 male non-athlete controls. Ultrasound measured shallow and deep layer thickness at 0%, 50% and 100% loading, and shear-wave elastography measured stiffness. The authors report that swimmers had the thickest heel fat pads at no load and the largest thickness change with loading in the shallow layer, and conclude that sport-specific loading may shape heel fat pad morphology and mechanics.
paper.tldr: In this small cross-sectional study, swimmers had the thickest heel fat pads at no load, and judo and American football athletes the thinnest. The authors suggest sport-specific loading may shape the heel fat pad, but they note that sport cannot be isolated as the only cause.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional comparison of 34 male university athletes (12 judo, 10 American football, 12 swimmers) and 12 male students with no sport participation. Ultrasound (14 MHz linear probe) measured shallow and deep layer thickness at 0%, 50% and 100% loading, and shear-wave elastography measured stiffness in the prone position. Participants with heel pain, recent foot or ankle injury or surgery, or rheumatic or systemic disease were excluded, and group differences were tested with ANOVA.
paper.findings: At no load, swimmers had the thickest shallow and deep layers (body-mass corrected), and the conclusions describe judo and American football athletes as thinnest; the discussion also reports controls thicker than judo and football, although one Results sentence reports the deep layer thicker in all three sports than in controls. Swimmers showed the greatest shallow-layer thickness change with loading, and judo and swimmers showed greater deep-layer change than American football from 0 to 50% load. Section 3.3 and the discussion report higher deep-layer stiffness in American football than in judo and swimmers and the highest shallow-layer stiffness in judo, which conflicts with the abstract and conclusions.
paper.limitations: The design is cross-sectional with 10 to 12 participants per group, controls were older than the athletes, and competitive history and measurement timing were not uniform. The stiffness results conflict: the abstract and conclusions place the lowest shallow-layer stiffness in American football and the highest deep-layer stiffness in swimmers, while Section 3.3 and the discussion place the highest deep-layer stiffness in American football and the highest shallow-layer stiffness in judo; the values here follow Section 3.3. The methods also describe controls both as non-participants in sport and as club athletes, do not clearly map the shallow and deep layers to the macro- and microchamber layers, and the study measured no pain or injury outcome.
paper.practicalImplications: Heel fat pad thickness and its response to load differed by sport in this small study, so sport-specific loading may be worth considering when heel pain is assessed in athletes. The study does not show that these differences predict pain or injury. Do not use the group values as reference ranges for individual athletes, given the small samples and the inconsistent stiffness results.
paper.athleteDev: The study measured tissue characteristics only and tested no training or performance outcome, so it cannot guide training prescription. Its relevance for performance staff is that heel tissue differed by sport in this sample, which could be tested in future work on load planning or footwear, as the authors discuss shoe wearing as one factor.
paper.rtp: The study compares athletes without heel pain or recent foot injury, and it does not evaluate injury, rehabilitation or return to sport. It should not be used to set return-to-sport criteria for heel pain.

records.sourceFile: Gait deviations associated with concussion - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Manaseer TS, Gross DP, Dennett L, Schneider K, Whittaker JL. Gait Deviations Associated With Concussion: A Systematic Review. Clin J Sport Med. 2020;30(2 Suppl 1):S11-S28.
paper.abstract: This systematic review identified quantifiable gait deviations associated with concussion across populations and time since injury. Six databases were searched from 1974 to 2016, and 21 analytic studies were included, all rated level 4 evidence with a median Downs and Black score of 12/33. The authors found consistent evidence of increased medial-lateral centre-of-mass displacement and inconsistent evidence of decreased gait velocity after concussion, with preliminary evidence that deficits may persist beyond 10 days.
paper.tldr: Concussed individuals in these studies swayed more side to side and sometimes walked more slowly than controls, and some deficits may last beyond the typical 10-day recovery period. The evidence is low-level, so gait testing should not yet be used alone to make concussion or return-to-activity decisions.
paper.methods: Systematic review following PRISMA guidance, with searches of six databases from January 1974 to September 2016. Two authors screened records independently and rated study quality with the Downs and Black checklist and the Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine levels. Meta-analysis was precluded by heterogeneity in gait parameters and in the timing of postconcussion testing.
paper.findings: The 21 included studies enrolled 1120 participants, most of them athletes or athletic-like students, and most compared concussed people with healthy controls. Medial-lateral centre-of-mass displacement was reported as increased in concussed groups in multiple studies, and gait velocity was reported as decreased in some studies but not others. Several studies reported gait deviations after the typical 10-day recovery period, and three reported deviations after return to activity, but these findings rest on fewer studies.
paper.limitations: Study quality was low, with a median Downs and Black score of 12/33 and the main threats being selection bias and poor adjustment for confounders. Fifteen studies (71%) had fewer than 50 participants, and 76% were conducted by three research teams, which limits generalisability. The authors also state that the timing of follow-up testing was not justified and that only two studies reported the measurement properties of their systems.
paper.practicalImplications: Gait assessment may be considered as one part of a concussion evaluation, and the authors say a clinical gait test should include walking speed and side-to-side sway. Because the evidence is low-level and inconsistent, staff should not rely on a single gait measure to decide when an athlete is recovered. The authors note that the common Tandem Gait Test captures both elements, but its accuracy for detecting gait disturbance is unknown.
paper.athleteDev: Not applicable. This review addresses concussion and gait in injury assessment and does not study training, performance or performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: The authors state that no included study assessed gait parameters to inform return to activity, sport, recreation or work decisions. The review supports only the finding that some gait deficits may persist after the typical 10-day recovery period, and it should not be used to set return-to-play criteria.

records.sourceFile: Genetic Susceptibility to Sport-Related Muscle Injuries - Insights from the Literature and Novel Gene Candidates.pdf

paper.citation: Leońska-Duniec A. Genetic Susceptibility to Sport-Related Muscle Injuries: Insights from the Literature and Novel Gene Candidates. Int J Mol Sci. 2025;26:11175.
paper.abstract: This review summarises polymorphisms associated with susceptibility to sport-related muscle injury in physically active people, identified through a systematic search of PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science. The author reports that 37 single nucleotide polymorphisms in 32 genes have been linked to injury risk, recurrence, severity and recovery. The genes cluster into functional categories, and the review proposes candidate genes for future work.
paper.tldr: Several gene variants, including ACTN3 R577X, ACE I/D and COL5A1 rs12722, have been associated with muscle injury in some studies, but findings are inconsistent and mostly come from case-control studies of one or a few SNPs. Nothing in the review validates a genotype or score for screening athletes or setting individual injury risk.
paper.methods: Literature review with a described search of PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science using polymorphism, gene, SNP and muscle injury terms. Inclusion criteria were original English-language human studies in physically active people with documented muscle injuries, excluding people with additional disease. No search dates, study counts, selection flow, pooled analysis or formal quality appraisal are reported.
paper.findings: The review reports 37 SNPs in 32 genes associated with muscle injury risk, incidence, severity or recovery time. It cites a systematic review in which the ACTN3 XX genotype was linked to noncontact muscle injury in 12 of 13 studies, while other studies found no association, and IL6 rs1800795 findings point in opposite directions (GG as the risk genotype in one study, CC in another). For ACE, the II genotype is linked to more muscle injuries in football players and the D allele to protection, and a 4-SNP total genotype score in 64 Italian footballers gave an injury odds ratio of 3.5 above a 56.2 a.u. cut-off.
paper.limitations: Most of the included evidence comes from case-control studies of one or a few SNPs, which the author says do not support firm conclusions about combined effects. The review does not describe quality appraisal or pooled effect sizes, and the Table 2 candidate genes were selected mainly on biological plausibility rather than tested for muscle injury. COL5A1 rs12722 is described inconsistently (Table 1 lists the CT genotype with greater severity and TT as lower risk, while the text describes TT as stiffer and higher risk).
paper.practicalImplications: Current findings do not support using a genotype to screen athletes or to predict an individual's muscle injury risk. The author suggests that multi-gene scores, genome-wide and sequencing studies, and epigenetic work could support personalised prevention in future. Until such work is validated, staff should treat genetic results as research information rather than as a basis for training or selection decisions.
paper.athleteDev: The review links some variants to performance traits, such as the ACTN3 RR genotype in speed and power athletes and the ACE D allele with power and strength, but these links are not injury tools. Use this evidence as background only, and do not use genotype to select, rank or limit athletes.
paper.rtp: The review does not evaluate return to sport or rehabilitation outcomes. Reported links between some variants and longer recovery time come from individual association studies and cannot be used to set rehabilitation or return-to-play timelines.

records.sourceFile: Genetic Variants and Hamstring Injury in Soccer- An Association and Validation Study.pdf

paper.citation: Larruskain J, Celorrio D, Barrio I, Odriozola A, Gil SM, Fernandez-Lopez JR, et al. Genetic Variants and Hamstring Injury in Soccer: An Association and Validation Study. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2017. Published ahead of print.
paper.abstract: This study investigated candidate SNPs associated with non-contact hamstring injury in elite soccer players and tested a risk model in an independent season. Five SNPs (MMP3, TNC, IL6, NOS3, HIF1A) and age were associated with hamstring injury in the discovery phase, with a C index of 0.74. The model did not predict injury in the validation season (C index 0.52), and the authors conclude that genetic testing for hamstring injury risk seems premature.
paper.tldr: Five gene variants and age were associated with hamstring injury in one elite club over five seasons, but the resulting risk model could not identify injured players in the following season. Genetic testing for hamstring risk is not yet supported.
paper.methods: Prospective cohort of 107 male outfield players from one elite club (First team, Reserves and U19), with time-loss hamstring injuries and exposure recorded over six seasons; saliva for genotyping was collected in 2014-2015. Players were genotyped for 37 SNPs, each tested under four inheritance models with the best chosen by minimum P, and variables with P of 0.25 or less entered a forward-selection Cox proportional hazards model with frailty terms in the discovery seasons (2010-2011 to 2014-2015). Discrimination was tested with Harrell's C index in the discovery phase and in the 2015-2016 validation season.
paper.findings: In the discovery phase, MMP3 rs679620 (A vs G, HR 2.06, 95% CI 1.51-2.81), TNC rs2104772 (A vs T, HR 1.65, 95% CI 1.17-2.32), IL6 rs1800795 (GG vs GC+CC, HR 1.68, 95% CI 1.11-2.53), NOS3 rs1799983 (G vs T, HR 1.35, 95% CI 1.01-1.79) and HIF1A rs11549465 (CC vs CT, HR 2.08, 95% CI 1.00-4.29) were associated with hamstring injury in the multivariable model, as was age of 24 or older (HR 2.10, 95% CI 1.29-3.42). TNC and IL6 were not significant on their own (P = 0.12 and 0.25), and MMP3 rs679620 was the only SNP associated with acute, overuse, severe and recurrent injuries separately. The model had a C index of 0.74 in discovery and 0.52 in validation.
paper.limitations: Only one club was studied, and the authors state that replication is needed. The validation phase included 31 injuries from 67 players, and the injury subtype analyses were underpowered. Preventive training was not recorded, and two SNPs (COL1A1 rs1800012 and COL5A1 rs12722) had 10% missing genotypes. The HIF1A confidence interval reaches 1.00, and no correction for multiple testing across 37 SNPs and several inheritance models is described. The study was funded by Baigene, a genetics company, and several authors are its members.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not use these genotypes to identify hamstring injury risk in players. The model did not predict injury in an independent season, so the flagged variants should be treated as research leads. Hamstring prevention programmes should continue to be offered to all players, as the authors recommend, because screening tests are not yet accurate.
paper.athleteDev: Not applicable. The study addresses injury susceptibility and does not examine performance outcomes or training adaptation.
paper.rtp: The study models the risk of any hamstring injury, including recurrences, and does not examine rehabilitation or return to play. Its findings cannot be used to set return-to-play timelines or to guide rehabilitation decisions after injury.

records.sourceFile: Genetic and epigenetic determinants of injury risk and recovery in elite athletes - Toward precision sports medicine.pdf

paper.citation: Ding H, Deng Q, Guo Z. Genetic and epigenetic determinants of injury risk and recovery in elite athletes: toward precision sports medicine. Gene. 2026;980:149957.
paper.abstract: This review synthesises genetic and epigenetic determinants of injury risk and recovery in elite athletes. It covers candidate SNPs in COL1A1, COL5A1, ACTN3 and IL6, genome-wide association studies, polygenic risk scores (PRS), DNA methylation and exercise-responsive microRNAs. The authors conclude that current genetic associations should be viewed as probabilistic and require multi-ethnic validation before clinical translation.
paper.tldr: Genetic and epigenetic markers such as COL5A1, MMP3, ACTN3 and some microRNAs have been linked to injury or recovery, but the review describes these links as probabilistic and much of the cited evidence is not from elite athletes. Polygenic risk scores are presented as research tools rather than ready-to-use screening instruments.
paper.methods: Narrative synthesis of literature retrieved from PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science using keywords such as genetics, sports injuries, recovery, epigenetics and nutrigenomics. English articles from 2000 to 2025 were considered, with emphasis on elite athlete cohorts, and both candidate-gene and GWAS studies were reviewed. The authors state that heterogeneity led them to present a narrative synthesis rather than a systematic review, and no inclusion criteria, pooled analysis or formal quality appraisal is described.
paper.findings: The review tabulates candidate variants and reports odds ratios from earlier meta-analyses, such as COL5A1 rs12722 TT vs TC+CC (OR 1.58, 95% CI 1.33-1.89; nine studies) for tendon and ligament injury. It describes a longitudinal pilot study of 64 professional Italian footballers in which injury risk was 3.5 times higher below a total genotype score cut-off of 56.2 a.u. It presents exercise-responsive microRNAs and DNA methylation as dynamic, context-dependent markers, and notes that existing PRS explain only 0.07% to 1.44% of variance in physical activity levels in UK Biobank data.
paper.limitations: The authors note small cohorts, limited population diversity, a lack of sport-specific validation, inconsistent definitions of non-responders, and methodological heterogeneity in methylation and microRNA studies. The review does not describe inclusion criteria or quality appraisal, so study selection cannot be checked. Some details are internally inconsistent: Table 1 attributes the COL1A1 meta-analysis to a different source than the text, and the MMP3 Achilles tendinopathy result is reported for a cohort described as ACL ruptures.
paper.practicalImplications: Current genetic and epigenetic results should not be used to screen athletes or to predict an individual's injury risk, since the authors describe PRS as research tools that are not ready for screening. Where genetic information is collected, the review says it should complement medical assessment and performance monitoring, not replace them. Staff should also plan for protection of athlete genetic data, which the review identifies as a privacy and discrimination risk.
paper.athleteDev: The review proposes that genotype could inform periodisation and that microRNA or methylation markers could track training adaptation. These are the authors' proposals drawn from small or early studies, so they should not change training prescriptions yet. Athletes should not be selected or ranked on genetic profiles.
paper.rtp: The review suggests that athletes with COL1A1 or COL5A1 variants might need longer recovery periods and that epigenetic markers could personalise rehabilitation. These are author proposals rather than tested findings, and they should not be used to set return-to-play timelines.

records.sourceFile: Genetic profile in genes associated with muscle injuries and injury etiology in professional soccer players.pdf

paper.citation: Maestro A, Del Coso J, Aguilar-Navarro M, Gutiérrez-Hellín J, Morencos E, Revuelta G, et al. Genetic profile in genes associated with muscle injuries and injury etiology in professional soccer players. Front Genet. 2022;13:1035899.
paper.abstract: This study examined the relationship between muscle injury-related genes and injury risk and etiology in 122 professional soccer players. Six polymorphisms were combined into a total genotype score (TGS), which was lower in injured players and had an odds ratio of 1.91 for injury at a cut-off of 45.83 a.u. The authors conclude that TGS may in future help predict injury risk in professional soccer players.
paper.tldr: A combined score of six muscle-related gene variants was lower in injured professional soccer players, but it discriminated injured from uninjured players only weakly. The score is not yet a usable injury predictor, and the single-season, single-cohort design limits what it can show.
paper.methods: Cohort of 122 Spanish male professional soccer players from five clubs during the 2021/2022 season, with a Caucasian-ancestry inclusion criterion and exclusion of players with incapacitating injuries in the previous 6 months. Six polymorphisms (ACE I/D, ACTN3, AMPD1, CKM, and two MLCK variants) were genotyped from buccal swabs, and a total genotype score was calculated. Non-contact injuries were recorded by club doctors using a consensus-based questionnaire, and TGS was compared between injured and non-injured players by t-test, chi-squared test, ROC analysis and logistic regression, with etiology analyses run across the 121 injuries.
paper.findings: Non-injured players had a mean TGS of 57.18 a.u. and injured players 51.71 a.u. (p = 0.034). ROC analysis gave an AUC of 0.612 (95% CI 0.513-0.711), and in the results players below the 45.83 a.u. cut-off had an odds ratio of 1.91 for injury (95% CI 1.14-2.91). AMPD1 CC genotype frequency was 88.2% in non-injured and 57.7% in injured players (p < 0.001), and TGS did not discriminate musculoskeletal injury, place of injury or injury severity.
paper.limitations: The study covers one season and five clubs, the sample is 122 players, the TGS cut-off was derived from the same data, and no correction for multiple testing is described. The abstract calls the design cross-sectional and the methods longitudinal, the abstract places higher risk beyond the cut-off while the results place it below, and the discussion gives a non-contact injury rate (16.6%) that conflicts with the results (58.2%). The discussion also compares MLCK CC in injured players (84.5%) with a 70.6% figure it attributes to AA players, though Table 5 gives 70.6% as CC in non-injured players, and it presents CKM GA and ACTN3 TT differences as findings although the overall tests were not significant (p = 0.131, 0.091 and 0.149).
paper.practicalImplications: Do not use the TGS or the AMPD1 and MLCK genotypes to identify players at risk of injury, since discrimination was weak and the findings have not been validated. The authors themselves say it is still premature to use genetic testing to predict injury risk in professional soccer players. Any future use would need replication in larger, multi-season cohorts.
paper.athleteDev: The study addresses injury susceptibility and not performance. The authors discuss muscle-performance genes, but the analysis does not measure performance, so the results should not be used to select or rank players.
paper.rtp: The study does not examine rehabilitation or return to play. Its finding that injury severity was not linked to the TGS in a discriminatory way means the score cannot inform recovery timelines or return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Genetic variants and ACL rupture -      A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Kaynak M, Nijman F, van Meurs J, Reijman M, Meuffels DE. Genetic Variants and Anterior Cruciate Ligament Rupture: A Systematic Review. Sports Med. 2017.
paper.abstract: This PRISMA systematic review summarised case-control evidence on genetic variants and anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture. Sixteen studies examining 33 variants were included and rated with a best-evidence synthesis. The authors found conflicting evidence for COL1A1 rs1800012 and COL3A1 rs1800255, limited evidence of no association for some COL5A1 and COL12A1 variants, and concluded that larger and prospective studies are needed.
paper.tldr: Sixteen case-control studies gave conflicting results for COL1A1 and COL3A1 variants and limited evidence against an association for some COL5A1 and COL12A1 variants. The authors conclude that the evidence does not yet show a clear genetic association with ACL rupture.
paper.methods: PRISMA-reported systematic review searching Embase, MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed Publisher, the Cochrane trials register and Google Scholar to 24 August 2015, with reference-list screening. Eligible studies were case-control, retrospective or prospective follow-up, or randomised designs comparing a genetic variant between ACL rupture cases and controls. Three reviewers assessed risk of bias with the Cochrane case-control tool, and pooling was not possible, so a best-evidence synthesis was used.
paper.findings: Sixteen case-control studies (eight high risk of bias, eight unclear) examined 33 variants. For COL1A1 rs1800012, two studies reported lower odds of rupture with the TT genotype (OR 0.12, 95% CI 0.02-0.92; OR 0.08, p = 0.031), one reported an association for GG (p = 0.046) and one found none. For COL3A1 rs1800255, AA vs GA+GG gave odds ratios of 3.8 (95% CI 1.1-12.8) and 5.05 (95% CI 1.62-15.78) in two Polish cohorts but no association in a South African cohort, and single-study findings for DCN rs516115 (GG protective) and VEGFA rs1570360 (GA harmful) rest on nearly the same population.
paper.limitations: Pooling was not possible because of heterogeneity in variants, outcome definitions and genetic contrasts. Many studies had small samples, 14 used partly or fully the same population for cases and controls, and eight were high risk of bias. Confounding by ethnicity is possible, and subgroup analyses by sex and injury mechanism could not be reported. The role of haplotypes remains unclear.
paper.practicalImplications: Current evidence does not support screening athletes for ACL rupture risk using these variants, because each variant has insufficient or conflicting evidence. Any future use would need large prospective studies that show predictive value. The review suggests genome-wide studies and studies of tendon and osteoarthritis genetics as next steps.
paper.athleteDev: Not applicable. The review addresses ACL rupture susceptibility and does not examine training, performance or performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: The review does not evaluate rehabilitation or return to sport. Its findings on injury susceptibility cannot inform return-to-play timelines or post-injury decisions after an ACL rupture.

records.sourceFile: Genetics and sport injuries - New perspectives for athletic excellence in an Italian court of rugby union players.pdf

paper.citation: Onori ME, Pasqualetti M, Moretti G, Canu G, De Paolis G, Baroni S, et al. Genetics and Sport Injuries: New Perspectives for Athletic Excellence in an Italian Court of Rugby Union Players. Genes. 2022;13:995.
paper.abstract: ACE, ACTN3, COL1A1 and MCT1 genotypes were compared between 100 male professional and semiprofessional rugby union players and 100 non-athletic Italian men, and related to injury history in the players. The authors report no significant genotype-injury association for ACE, ACTN3 or COL1A1. They report that the MCT1 rs1049434 AA genotype was associated with total and bone injuries, but the chi-square values they print (0.115 and 0.603) are inconsistent with the p-values given (0.003 and 0.007).
paper.tldr: In 100 rugby union players, the authors report that the MCT1 rs1049434 AA genotype was linked to total and bone injury history, while ACE, ACTN3 and COL1A1 were not. The result is small, unreplicated and internally inconsistent, so it does not support genetic screening of players.
paper.methods: Genotypes for ACE I/D, ACTN3 R577X, COL1A1 rs1800012 and MCT1 rs1049434 were determined by PCR, RFLP or Sanger sequencing in 100 male professional and semiprofessional rugby union players and 100 non-athletic Italian men. Injuries from medical history and injury records were grouped as bone, muscle or tendon/ligament, with genotype frequencies compared by chi-square tests and injured versus non-injured players compared by unpaired t-tests under a dominant model, at p < 0.05.
paper.findings: No genotype-injury association was reported for ACE, ACTN3 or COL1A1 (p > 0.05). For MCT1, the authors report that the AA genotype was associated with total injuries (reported chi-square 0.115, p = 0.003) and bone injuries (reported chi-square 0.603, p = 0.007), and allele frequencies did not differ between athletes and controls. The printed chi-square values do not correspond to the printed p-values, and no odds ratios or confidence intervals are given.
paper.limitations: The sample is small and drawn from two teams, with 15 athletes reporting no injuries, and injury data come from retrospective medical history and injury records. Four genes and several injury categories were tested with no multiple-comparison correction, an unpaired t-test was used to compare injured and non-injured players by genotype, and the injury counts by type (129 muscle, 247 bone, 170 tendon; sum 546) do not match the total of 573 reported. The control group is 100 non-athletic men over 18 with no age data reported, and the Hardy-Weinberg result is printed as p < 0.05, which conflicts with the stated equilibrium.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not use MCT1 genotype to screen players for injury risk or to set individual load, because the association is unreplicated and its statistics are inconsistent. Treat the MCT1 result as a hypothesis for prospective study in a larger squad with injuries recorded prospectively.
paper.athleteDev: This study does not support genotype-based talent selection or training individualisation. The ACE, ACTN3 and COL1A1 results are null, and the MCT1 result needs confirmation in a larger, prospectively followed squad.
paper.rtp: The study can speak to injury history by genotype, but not to return-to-sport decisions, since it does not assess rehabilitation, recovery time or return outcomes. Do not use the MCT1 result to set return-to-play timelines or clearance.

records.sourceFile: Groin Injuries in Soccer- Investigating the Effect of Age on Adductor Muscle Forces.pdf

paper.citation: Dupré T, Lysdal FG, Funken J, Mortensen KRL, Müller R, Mayer J, et al. Groin Injuries in Soccer: Investigating the Effect of Age on Adductor Muscle Forces. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2019 (published ahead of print).
paper.abstract: Sixty healthy male academy players in four age groups (U12, U15, U16 and U23) performed submaximal inside passes in a Footbonaut while motion capture and inverse dynamics estimated adductor longus and gracilis forces. Forces increased across age groups, and lower limb mass was the best anthropometric predictor of the calculated forces. The authors link this to overuse groin injury risk, which the study did not measure.
paper.tldr: In 60 academy players, modelled adductor forces during passing rose with age group, and lower limb mass tracked them best. No groin injuries were recorded, so the injury-risk link is an inference from the force estimates.
paper.methods: Sixty healthy male academy players (mean ages 11.1, 14.7, 15.8 and 20.2 years for U12, U15, U16 and U23) each performed 10 analysed inside passes in a Footbonaut, with 71 markers and 16 infrared cameras recording kinematics. An AnyBody model with static optimization estimated adductor longus and gracilis forces, and linear regression related those forces to thigh and lower limb size and mass.
paper.findings: Adductor longus and gracilis peak forces were significantly lower in U12 than in all older groups, and lower in U15 than in U16 and U23, while U16 and U23 did not differ significantly. Gracilis force rose 49% from U12 (92.4 N) to U15 (138.0 N), and adductor longus rose 22% from U15 to U16 and 6% from U16 to U23. Lower limb mass gave the highest R-squared for both muscles (0.70 for adductor longus and 0.73 for gracilis), above thigh mass (0.65 and 0.69) and lower limb length (0.51 and 0.54), and U15 players had lower hip flexion velocity than U12 and U16 and lower adduction velocity than U16 and U23.
paper.limitations: The design is cross-sectional, maturity was not measured, and group sizes of 14 to 17 mean that age, size and growth stage are confounded. The regression pools all 60 players, so the R-squared values largely reflect between-group size differences, and the forces are static optimization estimates checked only against EMG in earlier work. The abstract, Discussion and conclusion describe injury risk, reduced training volume and Copenhagen adduction training that the study did not test, and the conclusion names thigh mass where the regression favoured lower limb mass.
paper.practicalImplications: Lower limb mass should not yet be used as an injury-risk screen or to set training volume, because no injuries were recorded. The findings show that modelled adductor forces during passing rise through the academy years, which coaches could keep in mind when planning load changes; any screen would need testing against injury records.
paper.athleteDev: Modelled adductor forces during passing rose sharply between under-12 and under-15 players, so the demands of passing change through the academy years. The study estimated forces only and did not test how training volume or coaching alters them.
paper.rtp: The players were healthy, and no injured or rehabilitating players were studied, so the study cannot inform return-to-sport or rehabilitation decisions. It was not designed to test groin injury recovery.

records.sourceFile: Hamstring Injuries Risk Factors,                       Treatment, and Rehabilitation.pdf

paper.citation: Heer ST, Callander JW, Kraeutler MJ, Mei-Dan O, Mulcahey MK. Hamstring Injuries: Risk Factors, Treatment, and Rehabilitation. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2019;101(9):843-53.
paper.abstract: This Current Concepts Review covers the anatomy, risk factors, diagnosis, imaging, nonoperative and operative treatment, and rehabilitation of hamstring injuries. It summarises the published literature, includes a level-of-evidence table of selected studies, and grades its treatment recommendations.
paper.tldr: A previous hamstring injury is the strongest predictor of re-injury, and eccentric hamstring strengthening is recommended in both rehabilitation and prevention. Complete proximal avulsions with significant retraction are treated surgically, and other injuries are generally managed conservatively.
paper.methods: Narrative review of the literature on anatomy, risk factors, diagnosis, imaging, treatment and rehabilitation, with a level-of-evidence table (Table II) and recommendation grades (Table III). No search strategy is described.
paper.findings: Previous hamstring injury is the most predictive risk factor, with recurrence reported at 32% in American football, 21% in rugby and 16% in soccer. Eccentric physical therapy is recommended for rehabilitation, and Nordic hamstring exercise is cited as having a preventive effect in soccer players. Surgical repair of acute avulsions with retraction above 2.5 to 3 cm is graded B, and surgery for ischial tuberosity fractures displaced more than 1 cm is graded C.
paper.limitations: The review does not describe how sources were searched or appraised, and it draws on mixed populations and many lower-level studies. The authors note that return-to-preinjury criteria are hard to assess objectively, especially for grade 1 and 2 injuries.
paper.practicalImplications: For proximal tendon injuries, MRI is the most useful imaging study for injury extent and surgical planning. Eccentric hamstring tendon loading should be part of both nonoperative and postoperative rehabilitation, and the review cites Nordic exercise after training as preventive in soccer.
paper.athleteDev: Prior hamstring injury is the strongest flag for re-injury risk, so it should shape prevention priorities. Eccentric hamstring tendon strengthening belongs in both prevention and rehabilitation, but the review gives no loading or progression parameters.
paper.rtp: The review guides the choice between conservative and surgical care by injury type, favouring surgery for complete proximal avulsions with significant retraction. It states that return-to-preinjury criteria are hard to measure objectively, so it should not be the sole basis for clearance.

records.sourceFile: Hamstring Injury Mechanisms and Eccentric Training-Induced Muscle Adaptations - Current Insights and Future Directions.pdf

paper.citation: Andrews MH, Shield AJ, Lichtwark GA, Pincheira PA. Hamstring Injury Mechanisms and Eccentric Training-Induced Muscle Adaptations: Current Insights and Future Directions. Sports Med. 2025.
paper.abstract: This narrative review uses PubMed and SPORTDiscus searches to May 2025 to examine the causes of running-related hamstring injury, the effect of eccentric training on injury risk, and the contractile, non-contractile and neural adaptations to eccentric training. It argues that research has focused on resting fascicle length and that tendon, titin and neural adaptations need further study.
paper.tldr: Running-related hamstring injuries mostly occur in late swing, when the hamstrings produce large eccentric force at long lengths. Eccentric training, especially the Nordic exercise, reduces injury risk in adherent athletes, but the muscle changes that explain this protection remain unclear.
paper.methods: Narrative review with searches of PubMed and SPORTDiscus up to May 2025 using defined hamstring, injury mechanism, eccentric training and adaptation terms, followed by title and abstract screening and reference-list checks. Three predefined research questions shaped the scope.
paper.findings: Over 80% of hamstring injuries occur during high-speed running, mainly to the biceps femoris long head, with injury proposed in late swing or early stance.
