Meta-analytic evidence cited by the review indicates that Nordic programmes reduce injury incidence by about 51%; one meta-analysis found no significant effect, which the authors attribute to poor adherence, and restricting to compliant participants gave reductions approaching 65%. One prospective cohort cited by the review links each 0.5 cm of longer resting fascicle to a 21% lower injury risk, while the link between sarcomere, titin, tendon and neural changes and protection remains unverified.
paper.limitations: The review is narrative: it pools no data and does not grade the evidence. Several adaptation mechanisms rest on animal or non-hamstring studies, and the authors note that the link between resting fascicle lengthening and protection during active lengthening is theoretical.
paper.practicalImplications: Eccentric hamstring training should remain a core prevention approach, and adherence matters because the protective effects were concentrated in compliant participants. The review notes that knee-dominant exercises such as the Nordic tend to activate and grow the semitendinosus more than the biceps femoris long head, while hip-dominant exercises activate the hamstrings more uniformly, although surface EMG findings are inconsistent.
paper.athleteDev: Track adherence as a core metric for eccentric hamstring programmes, since protective effects were concentrated in players who completed them. Match exercise choice to the target region, although the review gives no dosing guidance.
paper.rtp: The review addresses prevention and training adaptation in running sports, not rehabilitation or return to play. Its conclusions cannot be used to set return-to-sport criteria or timeframes.

records.sourceFile: Hamstring Muscle Activity After Primary Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction—A Protective Mechanism in Those Who Do Not Sustain a Secondary Injury A Preliminary Study.pdf

paper.citation: Palmieri-Smith R, Strickland M, Lepley LK. Hamstring Muscle Activity After Primary Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: A Protective Mechanism in Those Who Do Not Sustain a Secondary Injury? A Preliminary Study. Sports Health. 2019.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study compared surface EMG of the vastus lateralis, biceps femoris and lateral gastrocnemius during a single-leg hopping task at return to play in 7 patients who later had a second ipsilateral ACL injury, 7 matched patients with a single ACL injury, and 7 uninjured controls. Hamstring activity before landing was higher in the single-injury group than in the re-injury group, and vastus lateralis activity after landing was lower in both ACL groups than in controls.
paper.tldr: At return to play after ACL reconstruction, patients who later re-injured the same knee used less hamstring activity before landing than those who did not, and all ACL patients used less vastus lateralis activity than controls. With 7 per group and a cross-sectional design, this is a hypothesis for prospective testing, not an established protective mechanism.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional study. Seven patients who later had a second ipsilateral ACL injury were matched 1:1 for sex, age (within 2 years), graft type and Tegner score to patients with a single ACL injury, and 7 uninjured controls were matched for sex and age (within 3 years). Participants performed single-leg hopping at return to play, with surface EMG normalised to peak dynamic activity and analysed 100 ms before and 250 ms after ground contact using ANOVA with post hoc t tests.
paper.findings: Pre-landing biceps femoris activity was 0.48 %max in the single-injury group and 0.20 %max in the re-injury group (P=0.018), with controls at 0.38 %max (not significant). After landing, vastus lateralis activity was 0.38 and 0.40 %max in the two ACL groups versus 0.58 %max in controls (P=0.016 and P=0.033). Quadriceps strength was lower in both ACL groups than in controls, and the groups did not differ on hamstring strength.
paper.limitations: The groups are very small, and the control group was significantly older than both ACL groups, which the authors acknowledge may reflect maturation effects. Only one hop task was used, and the authors state that the findings need longitudinal confirmation.
paper.practicalImplications: Rehabilitation after ACL reconstruction should keep targeting quadriceps (vastus lateralis) activity, since it was lower during landing in all reconstructed knees at return to play than in uninjured controls. Pre-landing hamstring activity is worth monitoring in future prospective studies, but this study does not show that training it reduces reinjury.
paper.athleteDev: Landing EMG at return to play could be explored as a monitoring idea, but this preliminary study gives no training dose or target. Hamstring pre-activation should not be used as a training target until prospective data confirm it.
paper.rtp: Landing muscle activity was lower in all ACL groups than in uninjured controls, which supports continued quadriceps-focused rehabilitation at return to play. The study does not establish clearance criteria, and the authors note that their return-to-play criteria differ from those recommended in the literature.

records.sourceFile: Hamstring and knee injuries are associated with isometric hip and trunk muscle strength in elite Australian Rules and Rugby League players.pdf

paper.citation: Hajek M, Williams MD, Bourne MN, Roberts LA, Morris NR, Shield AJ, et al. Hamstring and knee injuries are associated with isometric hip and trunk muscle strength in elite Australian Rules and Rugby League players. J Sci Med Sport. 2023 (journal pre-proof).
paper.abstract: This prospective cohort study measured isometric trunk and hip extensor strength (5 s maximal and 45 s endurance) and lumbar multifidus and quadratus lumborum cross-sectional area in AFL and NRL players during the 2020 preseason. Non-contact hamstring strain and knee ligament injuries were recorded over the season and analysed with logistic regression and decision trees.
paper.tldr: In elite AFL and NRL players, lower preseason trunk and hip extensor strength and endurance were associated with more hamstring strains. Larger lumbar multifidus size was associated with more knee ligament injuries, but the knee model did not discriminate well.
paper.methods: Prospective cohort. Isometric trunk and hip extensor strength was tested with a modified Biering-Sorensen protocol (5 s maximal and 45 s endurance), and lumbar multifidus and quadratus lumborum cross-sectional area was measured by ultrasound at the 2020 preseason. Injuries were recorded across the 2020 season, with univariable logistic regression (strength per SD) and decision trees with ROC analysis.
paper.findings: Of 126 players with follow-up, 19 had a hamstring strain and 13 a knee ligament injury. Per SD, maximal strength (OR 0.55, P=0.039) and strength endurance (OR 0.42, P=0.004) were associated with lower hamstring strain odds. Larger LM L5 CSA (OR 1.66 per cm2) and LM-to-QL ratio (OR 1.57) were associated with knee ligament injury (P=0.008 each), and no strength variable was associated with knee injury. The Results report decision-tree AUCs of 0.75 for hamstring and 0.82 for knee injury, but the Limitations describe the knee model as not discriminating.
paper.limitations: Injury numbers are small, 85 players declined the strength test, and the decision trees were not validated on held-out data; the Methods say no data were held back, while the Discussion mentions k-fold cross-validation. The Results give strength odds ratios per 1 N/kg while Table 2 gives them per SD, the Abstract gives a strength-endurance threshold in Nm while the Results give 3.42 N/kg, and the Results both state no differences and a higher BMI in players lost to follow-up.
paper.practicalImplications: The modified Biering-Sorensen field test gives a preseason measure of trunk and hip extensor strength and endurance that may help identify players at higher hamstring strain risk. The knee-ligament findings are exploratory and should not be used to screen players.
paper.athleteDev: Preseason trunk and hip extensor strength and endurance testing could support hamstring risk screening, since weaker players were more often injured here. The cut-offs are not validated, and lumbar muscle size should not be used to target knee injury screening on these data.
paper.rtp: The study addresses preseason injury risk, not return to play. It does not indicate when a player with a hamstring or knee injury is ready to return.

records.sourceFile: Hamstring exercises for track and field athletes -   Injury and exercise biomechanics and possible implication for   exercise selection and primary prevention.pdf

paper.citation: Malliaropoulos N, Mendiguchia J, Pehlivanidis H, Papadopoulou S, Valle X, Malliaras P, et al. Hamstring exercises for track and field athletes: injury and exercise biomechanics, and possible implications for exercise selection and primary prevention. Br J Sports Med. 2012;46:846-851.
paper.abstract: This review considers hamstring strain injuries in track and field athletes, the role of eccentric training in prevention, and the strength and biomechanical factors involved. It proposes exercise classification criteria (hip or knee dominance, kinetic chain, location, targeted muscle and training parameters) to guide prevention and strengthening programmes.
paper.tldr: Track and field hamstring prevention should emphasise eccentric strengthening, with exercises chosen by hip or knee dominance, kinetic chain and target muscle. The authors advise prioritising muscle length over strength or contraction speed, but the classification is a clinical proposal that has not been tested.
paper.methods: Narrative review of injury mechanisms (late swing and early stance sprinting), strength as a risk factor, the properties of eccentric training, prevention studies and exercise biomechanics. The authors propose an exercise classification and training principles for track and field; no search strategy is reported.
paper.findings: The review states that eccentric training consistently reduces hamstring injury rates, citing five prevention studies (four Nordic hamstring, one yo-yo curl) with over 1000 athletes, each reporting significant reductions. It recommends prioritising muscle length over strength and contraction velocity, combining open and closed kinetic chain and stretch-shortening exercises, and avoiding high-intensity, long-length eccentric work during key competition phases.
paper.limitations: No literature search is described, and no study is cited that compares eccentric protocols for preventing track and field hamstring injury. The authors say much of the training advice derives from basic science and clinical experience and needs randomised testing.
paper.practicalImplications: Include both hip-dominant and knee-dominant eccentric exercises, together with stretch-shortening exercises, rather than relying on a single exercise. Progress exposure to long-length strain gradually, and avoid high-intensity eccentric loading before key competitions, as the review recommends.
paper.athleteDev: The review gives coaches a framework for choosing hamstring exercises by hip or knee dominance, kinetic chain and target muscle, and for progressing strain. Its volume guidance is general, since no published track and field dose comparisons exist.
paper.rtp: The review addresses prevention and training design, not rehabilitation or return to sport, and it gives no clearance criteria.

records.sourceFile: Hamstring injuries - Prevention and treatment - An   update.pdf

paper.citation: Brukner P. Hamstring injuries: prevention and treatment, an update. Br J Sports Med. 2015;49:1241-1244.
paper.abstract: Narrative update on hamstring injuries. It reports that injury type (slow-stretch versus high-speed running) and central tendon involvement affect return-to-play time, that predictor evidence is conflicting, and that eccentric strength deficits may persist. It supports lengthened-position strengthening and NHE for prevention, and concludes that PRP is not yet supported for acute strains.
paper.tldr: Hamstring injuries still recur at high rates. Lengthened-position eccentric work and Nordic hamstring exercises are the main strategies discussed, and PRP is not yet supported by the evidence.
paper.methods: Narrative clinical review. No systematic search or appraisal method is described. The author discusses injury types, predictors of return to play, recurrence, rehabilitation programs, PRP trials and prevention studies.
paper.findings: Slow-stretch injuries and injuries involving the central tendon are reported to need longer return to play. Evidence for individual predictors, including MRI findings, is conflicting. Eccentric hamstring strength may remain reduced after return to play, and the two PRP trials gave conflicting results: a placebo-controlled trial found no benefit, while a non-placebo trial reported faster recovery with PRP. NHE programs are cited as reducing hamstring injury incidence.
paper.limitations: No search strategy or quality grading is given. The author acknowledges conflicting predictor evidence and few high-quality PRP trials, and some recommendations rest on mechanistic reasoning.
paper.practicalImplications: Classify injuries by mechanism and location, and expect longer return to play for slow-stretch and central tendon injuries. Include lengthened-position eccentric strengthening and NHE in rehabilitation and prevention, and do not expect PRP to shorten recovery on the strength of this review.
paper.athleteDev: Use injury type and recurrence risk to shape the return-to-running plan, and include NHE across the squad as a prevention method. Check eccentric hamstring strength after injury, since deficits may persist.
paper.rtp: Make lengthened-position strengthening a central part of rehabilitation and check eccentric strength before clearance. The review gives no validated RTP criteria, so injury type and clinical tests should guide timing.

records.sourceFile: Hamstring muscle elasticity differs in specialized high performance athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Avrillon S, Lacourpaille L, Hug F, Le Sant G, Frey A, Nordez A, et al. Hamstring muscle elasticity differs in specialized high-performance athletes. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2020;30:83-91.
paper.abstract: Compared passive shear modulus of the three hamstring muscles in elite athletes from seven sports with that of active controls, using shear wave elastography at 60 and 90 degrees of knee flexion. Semimembranosus stiffness was lower in four sports than in controls, while biceps femoris and semitendinosus did not differ.
paper.tldr: Semimembranosus stiffness was lower in some elite sports than in controls, and the authors link the pattern to stretching demands in taekwondo, figure skating, fencing and soccer. Biceps femoris and semitendinosus did not differ.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional study. Participants lay supine with the hip flexed to 90 degrees while the knee was held at 90 and 60 degrees on an isokinetic dynamometer. Shear modulus was measured by shear wave elastography, with inter-day reliability assessed in 12 controls (ICC 0.80 to 0.98). Athletes with a unilateral injury history contributed only their uninjured leg, and ANOVA models compared groups and muscles.
paper.findings: At 60 degrees, semimembranosus shear modulus was lower than in controls in figure skating (mean difference -17.2 kPa, d = 1.8), taekwondo (-18.0 kPa, d = 2.1), fencing (-10.3 kPa, d = 1.0) and soccer (-9.0 kPa, d = 0.9). No difference was found for sprinters, field hockey or basketball players. Biceps femoris and semitendinosus did not differ between athletes and controls, and sex had no main effect.
paper.limitations: The design cannot separate sport effects from innate properties, prior injury or stretching volume, which was not quantified. Group sizes are small, and basketball players were 9.7 years younger than controls. The conclusion says semimembranosus shear modulus is 'increased' in these athletes, which conflicts with the lower values in the abstract and results; this summary follows the results. Between-person variation is large, with SD up to 44% of the mean at 60 degrees.
paper.practicalImplications: Interpret hamstring stiffness profiles against sport-specific norms, because semimembranosus values differed by sport. Do not compare an athlete's values with a general reference population without that sport context.
paper.athleteDev: Sports with long stretching demands may show lower semimembranosus stiffness, which may be a training adaptation rather than a deficit. Whether it affects performance is not shown, so it should not set a training target.
paper.rtp: Not for return-to-sport decisions or injury risk. The study excluded injured sides and did not follow athletes after injury, so it says nothing about stiffness during recovery.

records.sourceFile: Hamstring muscle stiffness in athletes with and without anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction history - A retrospective study.pdf

paper.citation: Kepir E, Demiral F, Akaras E, Paksoy AE, Sevindik Aktas B, Yilmaz Cankaya B, et al. Hamstring muscle stiffness in athletes with and without anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction history: a retrospective study. J Clin Med. 2024;13:4370.
paper.abstract: Retrospective case-control comparison of passive hamstring stiffness, measured with shear wave elastography, in athletes with and without ACL reconstruction history. Stiffness of the biceps femoris long head, semimembranosus and semitendinosus did not differ between injured legs, uninjured contralateral legs and control legs.
paper.tldr: Passive mid-belly hamstring stiffness did not differ between legs of athletes after ACL reconstruction and legs of uninjured athletes. The study is small and retrospective, and it measured only the mid-belly.
paper.methods: Retrospective comparative case-control design. With the participant prone and relaxed, three mid-belly elastograms per muscle were averaged; groups were compared by one-way ANOVA. The injured group was 13 athletes aged 18 to 35 who had returned to sport after ACL reconstruction with a semitendinosus graft; the control group was 20 uninjured athletes contributing both legs.
paper.findings: Mean stiffness was similar across groups for all three muscles, with reported p values of 0.291 or higher. For example, biceps femoris long head was 26.19 kPa in injured legs, 26.16 kPa in uninjured contralateral legs and 27.64 kPa in control legs. The hypothesis of higher semitendinosus stiffness from post-surgical scar tissue was not supported.
paper.limitations: The design is retrospective, with an unblinded assessor, unmeasured probe pressure and no reliability study. Only male athletes were included, and rehabilitation details could not be recorded. The three small measurement points sat in the lowest-stiffness (blue) region, the sample size was based on an assumed large effect (0.8), and the discussion quotes a BFlh value of 9.91 kPa for this study that does not match the 26 to 28 kPa in Table 1.
paper.practicalImplications: Mid-belly stiffness measured this way did not separate ACL-reconstructed athletes from uninjured athletes, so it should not be used as a marker of post-ACL hamstring change. Anyone using elastography should record probe pressure and region-of-interest size, and check reliability locally.
paper.athleteDev: This study does not show a change in hamstring stiffness after ACL reconstruction, so it gives no performance target. It also did not link stiffness to performance or hamstring strain risk.
paper.rtp: Do not use these results to set return-to-sport criteria after ACL reconstruction, since stiffness did not differ from controls and recovery was not tracked. The study cannot show whether elastography can monitor healing, which the authors suggest but did not test.

records.sourceFile: Hamstring reinjuries occur at the same location and   early after return to sport - A descriptive study of MRI   confirmed reinjuries.pdf

paper.citation: Wangensteen A, Tol JL, Witvrouw E, Van Linschoten R, Almusa E, Hamilton B, et al. Hamstring reinjuries occur at the same location and early after return to sport: a descriptive study of MRI-confirmed reinjuries. Am J Sports Med. 2016;44(8):2112-2121.
paper.abstract: This descriptive case series drew on 180 male athletes who had an MRI within 5 days of an acute hamstring injury, and analysed the 19 MRI-confirmed reinjuries in the same leg within one year of return to sport (18 football and 1 futsal player). Most of the reinjuries (15 of 19, 79%) occurred in the same location as the index injury, more than half (10 of 19) occurred within 25 days of return to sport, and all 7 reinjuries that were more severe on MRI grading occurred in the same location. The authors suggest the index injury may not have healed completely and recommend reinjury-prevention exercise after return to sport.
paper.tldr: Most hamstring reinjuries in this series happened in the same place as the original injury and within weeks of return to sport. Keep hamstring-specific loading going after return to sport, because the injury may not have fully healed.
paper.methods: Descriptive case series within a prospective cohort and randomised trial at Aspetar, Doha. An MRI was taken five days after the index injury in 180 athletes, and athletes were followed for one year after return to sport; reinjury required acute posterior thigh pain and MRI signal change. A single radiologist scored index and reinjury location and severity, and medians and proportions were reported.
paper.findings: Of the 19 reinjuries, 15 (79%) were in the same muscle and location as the index injury, and the musculotendinous junction was the most common reinjury site (13 of 19). The median time from return to sport to reinjury was 24 days (range 4-311), and 10 of 19 reinjuries occurred within 25 days of return to sport. Seven of 19 reinjuries (37%) were graded more severe on MRI than the index injury, and all seven were in the same location; continuous MRI measures of injury extent did not differ between index injury and reinjury.
paper.limitations: The study is single-centre with only 19 reinjuries and no comparison group, and percentages are of those 19 reinjuries rather than the 180 athletes. Return-to-sport decisions outside the study centre varied, 74 athletes were followed only passively so some reinjuries may have been missed, and the authors note that same-location MRI signal may partly reflect residual index injury rather than a new reinjury.
paper.practicalImplications: After return to sport, continue specific hamstring loading and reinjury-prevention work, particularly in the first few weeks, because most reinjuries in this series were early and in the original location. Note that the paper cannot show whether a particular return-to-sport test or time frame prevents reinjury.
paper.athleteDev: The paper has no performance outcomes. Its practical message is to keep hamstring-specific training going after return to sport, since reinjuries clustered in the original location early on.
paper.rtp: The study can inform the period after return to sport, showing that reinjury risk was high in the first weeks and that reinjury was usually in the original location. It cannot be used to set a validated return-to-sport criterion, because the authors state that no objective validated criteria exist and this study did not test any.

records.sourceFile: Hamstrings are Stretched More and Faster during Accelerative Running Compared to Speed-Matched Constant-Speed Running.pdf

paper.citation: Gurchiek RD, Teplin Z, Falisse A, Hicks JL, Delp SL. Hamstrings are stretched more and faster during accelerative running compared to speed-matched constant-speed running. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2024. Published ahead of print.
paper.abstract: Ten recreationally active adults ran at constant speeds and in accelerative flying sprints, and OpenCap markerless motion capture with a musculoskeletal model estimated biceps femoris long head muscle-tendon length and lengthening velocity. Peak length was greater in accelerative running below 75% of top speed, and lengthening velocity was greater in accelerative running at all speeds. Greater hip flexion drove the longer lengths and faster lengthening, and the knee's contribution was smaller during acceleration.
paper.tldr: During acceleration from slower speeds, the modelled biceps femoris was stretched further and lengthened faster than at the same constant speed. Staff monitoring hamstring exposure may need to count acceleration, not only top speed.
paper.methods: Ten recreationally active participants recorded overground trials at self-selected jogging and brisk speeds and prescribed speeds of 3, 4, 5 and 6 m/s, each as constant-speed running and as an accelerative flying sprint, with a 30 m maximal sprint to set top speed. OpenCap and a three-dimensional musculoskeletal model estimated peak muscle-tendon length and step-average lengthening velocity. Linear mixed models compared the conditions across running speeds.
paper.findings: At top speed, peak muscle-tendon length was 111-112% of neutral length and did not differ between conditions (p=0.431). Below about 75% of top speed, accelerative running gave longer peak lengths (p<0.001), and the regression model predicted that accelerating from 50% of top speed produced the same peak length as constant running at 88%. Average lengthening velocity was greater during acceleration at all speeds, driven by faster hip flexion rather than knee extension. During acceleration, peak length occurred at an average hip flexion angle of 67 degrees regardless of speed, and at slower speeds both hip and knee were more flexed at peak length than in constant-speed running.
paper.limitations: The sample was small (n=10, 5 men and 5 women) and not all participants were sprint specialists. Muscle length and velocity are model estimates from markerless video, OpenCap has not been validated for these specific tasks, speed order was not randomised, and 61 of 300 steps were removed in quality control. Only the swing-phase step was analysed, and the authors state that causal links between acceleration mechanics and hamstring injury are not established.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff who track hamstring exposure with running speed alone may miss the high lengths and fast lengthening that occur when players accelerate from slower speeds. Consider counting acceleration as well as speed when planning exposure, while recognising that the link to injury has not been shown.
paper.athleteDev: The paper gives no performance outcome. Its findings suggest that acceleration from slower speeds loads the hamstrings with longer, faster lengthening than constant running at the same speed, which may matter when designing acceleration training.
paper.rtp: The study cannot inform return to sport, because it included no injured athletes and no rehabilitation or return-to-running outcomes. It can only describe modelled hamstring mechanics in healthy recreationally active adults.

records.sourceFile: Higher hamstrings strength and stability are related to lower kinematics alteration during running after central and peripheral fatigue.pdf

paper.citation: Encarnación-Martínez A, García-Gallart A, Sanchis-Sanchis R, Jimenez-Perez I, Priego-Quesada JI, Pérez-Soriano P. Higher Hamstrings Strength and Stability Are Related to Lower Kinematics Alteration during Running after Central and Peripheral Fatigue. Sensors. 2022;22:1990.
paper.abstract: Eighteen male recreational runners had hamstring and quadriceps isokinetic strength and dynamic postural stability measured, then ran kinematic trials before and after central and peripheral fatigue protocols. Runners with higher hamstring strength and better stability showed smaller kinematic changes after central fatigue, and smaller ankle changes after peripheral fatigue.
paper.tldr: In 18 male recreational runners, those with stronger hamstrings and better jump-landing stability showed smaller changes in running mechanics after fatigue. These are associations in a small laboratory study, so they do not show that strength training reduces fatigue-related changes.
paper.methods: Within-subject laboratory study with 18 male recreational runners (no injury in the prior 6 months) who completed central fatigue (30 minutes of treadmill running at 85% of maximal aerobic speed) and peripheral fatigue (continuous isokinetic knee flexion-extension until peak torque fell below 50%) sessions in randomized order. Isokinetic peak torque, a jump-landing dynamic postural stability index, and treadmill kinematics before and after each fatigue protocol were analyzed with repeated-measures ANOVA or Friedman tests and Pearson correlations.
paper.findings: After central fatigue, knee flexion at maximum knee flexion rose from 32.12 to 33.79 degrees (p < 0.01), stance time from 0.226 to 0.232 s (p = 0.025) and propulsion time from 0.127 to 0.133 s (p = 0.033). After peripheral fatigue, knee flexion at toe-off rose (p = 0.003) and ankle angle at initial contact moved toward plantarflexion (p = 0.035). Runners with greater hamstring torque had smaller knee-flexion change after central fatigue (r = -0.582), and a worse stability index was linked to larger knee-flexion change (r = 0.534).
paper.limitations: Eighteen runners is a small sample, and most findings are Pearson correlations across many outcomes, so the results are exploratory. Several correlations are reported with p values smaller than a sample of 18 would usually give, and the unit of analysis for these correlations is not stated. The 113.6 N reduction in ground reaction force is estimated from earlier literature rather than measured, the sample size calculation refers to cyclists although runners were tested, and no training program or injury outcome was studied.
paper.practicalImplications: Hamstring strength and jump-landing stability testing may help identify runners whose technique changes more when fatigued, which could guide monitoring. The study does not show that training these qualities reduces fatigue-related changes or injury risk, so present any training recommendation as untested.
paper.athleteDev: For recreational runners, greater hamstring strength and better dynamic stability were associated with smaller fatigue-related changes in knee flexion and stance time. The study does not show that training these qualities would prevent those changes.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested healthy recreational runners with no injury, and it reports no rehabilitation or return-to-running outcomes.

paper.citation: Taylor JB, Nguyen AD, Shultz SJ, Ford KR. Hip biomechanics differ in responders and non-responders to an ACL injury prevention program. Knee Surgery, Sports Traumatology, Arthroscopy. 2018.
paper.abstract: Adolescent female athletes in the intervention arm of a cluster-randomized trial (43 reported, 42 in the responder analysis) completed drop vertical jump testing before and after a 6-week ACL injury prevention program. Athletes whose knee abduction moment fell beyond the minimal detectable change had greater hip adduction excursion at baseline and larger improvements in hip flexion and knee abduction measures, while the program overall did not reduce knee abduction moment relative to control.
paper.tldr: Adolescent female athletes who reduced knee valgus loading most in a 6-week warm-up injury prevention program started with greater hip adduction and showed larger hip flexion changes. The comparison involved only eight responders, and the program as a whole did not outperform control, so this does not yet validate a test for who will respond.
paper.methods: Secondary analysis of a cluster-randomized trial in which female basketball and soccer players aged 13 to 19 years completed a 20 to 25 minute warm-up-based program 2 to 3 times a week for 6 weeks. Within the intervention arm, responders were athletes whose knee abduction moment fell by more than 9.4 N m (the minimal detectable change) on a drop vertical jump, and baseline and change scores for 3D hip and knee kinematics and kinetics, performance tests and history variables were compared with MANOVA, t tests and chi-square tests.
paper.findings: At baseline, responders showed greater hip adduction excursion than non-responders (5.3 vs 2.7 degrees, p = 0.02, d = 0.82), with no other baseline biomechanical differences. Responders reduced knee abduction moment by 17.8 N m versus an increase of 2.5 N m in non-responders (p < 0.001), and increased peak hip flexion angle (+5.1 vs -1.2 degrees, p = 0.02) and hip flexion moment (+37.8 vs +4.2 N m, p < 0.001). Responders attended about 22% more sessions and were more often soccer players, both trends (p = 0.07), and the intervention group as a whole did not differ from control in knee abduction moment change.
paper.limitations: Only 8 responders were compared with 34 non-responders, and the analysis is a post-hoc sub-analysis of a trial powered for the overall comparison. Responders were defined by the same knee abduction moment change that is then compared between groups, so part of that difference follows from the grouping, and the authors note classification by one variable as a limitation. The tables sum to 42 athletes, while the abstract and methods report 43 in the intervention arm, and the text does not explain the difference.
paper.practicalImplications: Before a warm-up injury prevention program, clinicians may record hip adduction excursion with frontal-plane video, as the authors suggest, to flag athletes who may need more individualized work. Because the baseline finding rests on eight responders and has not been tested as a predictor, treat it as a hypothesis rather than a screening cut-off.
paper.athleteDev: In adolescent female basketball and soccer players, those whose knee abduction moment fell meaningfully after a 6-week warm-up program had started with greater hip adduction excursion and also increased hip flexion angle and moment. Team-wide warm-up programs may not change landing mechanics equally across players, but the study does not show effects on performance or injury.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested healthy adolescent athletes without a current lower-extremity injury, and it reports no rehabilitation or return-to-play outcomes.
